neighbours.label: The exclamation ' Oh'/' oh' breaking into narrative after a completed sentence or clause ('... village? Oh, his voice', 'When, oh! the welcome news'), in old-fashioned literary prose or verse; weaker on a hortative ' Come'
fire: The letter lay three days unopened upon the table, for none dared break the seal. Oh! what tidings it held for that poor household.
I looked for my brother among the men who came down from the ship. Oh, he was not there, and my heart sank within me.

The storm had raged for half the night,
And all our hope was gone,
When, oh! a sail came into sight,
And bore us safely on.
She had promised to return before the leaves fell from the old elm. Oh! how long that autumn seemed to those who waited.

We climbed the hill at break of day,
And rested by the stone,
And, oh! the valley far away
Lay golden in the sun.
The good old doctor shook his head and spoke no word of comfort to us. Oh, it was a bitter hour for my mother.
They told me that the house was sold and the garden ploughed under. Oh! I could have wept to hear it.
The children ran before us to the gate where their father stood waiting. Oh, what a welcome he gave them that evening.
quiet: The letter lay three days unopened upon the table, for none dared break the seal. Nobody guessed what tidings it held for that poor household.
I looked for my brother among the men who walked down from the ship. But he was not there, and my heart sank within me.

The storm had raged for half the night,
And all our hope was gone,
When far away a sail was seen,
And bore us safely on.
She had promised to return before the leaves fell from the old elm. That autumn seemed very long to those who waited.

We climbed the hill at break of day,
And rested by the stone,
And saw the valley far away
Lie golden in the sun.
The good old doctor shook his head and spoke no word of comfort to us. It was a bitter hour for my mother.
They told me that the house was sold and the garden ploughed under. I could have wept to hear it.
The children ran before us to the gate where their father stood waiting. He gave them a warm welcome that evening.

notes: Card: ' Oh' x4, ' oh' x3, ' came' x3, 'Come' x2 in 18th-19th century prose and verse. Probes: needs earlier context; one-clause 'cried, Oh, what shall I do!' only 0.09, but after a full sentence 'Oh! how the hours dragged' 0.52, 'Oh, it was gone' 0.31, verse 'When, oh! the light' 1.12, 'Come, away!' 0.22; the same passage with 'Then' 0.19.
